---
title: 5 - Vector styles
---

## 5.1. 

The Tanzania Forest Rerserves 2022 layer contains four different sub-categories of forest reserves. At the moment, these categories are not distinguished, but the layer is visualised with just one single style. Let's create an attribute-based styling to visualise each category with a different color.

The forest reserve sub-categories are stored in attribute called `desig`, short for *designation*:
- Forest Reserve
- Forest Plantation
- Nature Forest Reserve
- Village Land Forest Reserve

This rule-based styling is a bit complicated in OpenLayers. Some plugins provide neat ways to do this, but in this tutorial we concentrate on the basics and working without plugins. At the end of this tutorial, we link some handy plugins for you to explore that may easen your work in the future. 

- [ ] Open `main.js` and paste the code block below just after the imports:

```javascript
main.js

// Forest reserve styles based on the 'desig' attribute
const forestStyles = {
  'Forest Reserve': new Style({
    fill: new Fill({
      color: '#006b00'
    }),
    stroke: new Stroke({
      color: '#006b00',
      width: 1
    })
  }),

  'Forest Plantation': new Style({
    fill: new Fill({
      color: '#d3f226'
    }),
    stroke: new Stroke({
      color:'#d3f226',
      width: 1
    })
  }),

  'Nature Forest Reserve': new Style({
    fill: new Fill({
      color: '#81bf00'
    }),
    stroke: new Stroke({
      color: '#81bf00',
      width: 1
    })
  }),

  'Village Land Forest Reserve': new Style({
    fill: new Fill({
      color: '#56cf68'
    }),
    stroke: new Stroke({
      color: '#56cf68',
      width: 1
    })
  })
};
```

As you can see, each category is displayed separately, and contains parameters for 
- `fill` that controls the polygon interior,
- `stroke` that controls the polygon outline, and
- `width` that controls the outline thickness. 

The fill and outline colors are just black at this point. 
- [ ] Change them for each category based on the HTML color codes below:

- Forest Reserve: #006b00
- Forest Plantation: #d3f226
- Nature Forest Reserve: #81bf00
- Village Land Forest Reserve: #56cf68

Next, we must tell how the visualisations are applied to the layer where these categories are stored in the `desig` attribute. This can be done with a simple function below.

- [ ] Copythe code block below and paste it to your `main.js` file, right after the code that creates the styling:

```
main.js

function forestReserveStyleFunction(feature) {
  return forestStyles[feature.get('desig')] || null;
};
```
::: {.callout-note}
The `null` statement is added to prevent breakage of the whole visualisation. If you have a typo e.g. in one of the forest reserve categories, the visualisation for that category appears as `null`, i.e. transparent on the map, instead of breaking the whole visualisation for the layer.
:::



## 5.2. Apply the newly created style for the correct layer

Defining a style does not automatically change the map. We must also assign the style function to the correct vector layer. So far, your new style is defined and exists, but it is not applied on any layer.

- [ ] Scroll down to the layer list where you have defined the GeoJSON layers. Here, you'll need to add one additional parameter that tells the `tanzania_forest_reserves_2022` layer to use the style you just created:

```javascript
main.js

  new VectorLayer({
    source: new VectorSource({
      format: new GeoJSON(),
      url: './data/tanzania_forest_reserves_2022.json'
    }),
    style: forestReserveStyleFunction
  }),
```

Save and check how the webmap looks like. Do you distinguish the different forest reserve categories?


## 5.3. Create style for the National parks layer

Colours are useful for distinguishing categories, but patterns can also help differentiate overlapping polygon layers. The *Tanzania World Heritage and Ramsar Sites 2026* layer already uses a diagonal hatch pattern, drawn to your map from its styling in GeoServer. 

We will create a similar pattern for *Tanzania National parks and Conservation areas 2023* layer, but using the opposite diagonal direction. When these two layers overlap, there will be a "net" pattern displayed on the map.

Once again, this fill pattern style is a bit complicated to create in OpenLayers.

- [ ] Copy the whole code block below and paste it to your `main.js` file, right after the `function` that defines the forest reserves style:

```javascript
main.js

// Create a diagonal hatch pattern used to symbolize national parks and conservation areas
function createHatchPattern() {
  const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
  canvas.width = 10;
  canvas.height = 10;

  const context = canvas.getContext('2d');

  //Draw diagonal hatch line
  context.strokeStyle = '#000000';
  context.lineWidth = 2;

  context.beginPath();
  context.moveTo(0, 0);
  context.lineTo(10, 10);
  context.stroke();

  return context.createPattern(canvas, 'repeat');
}

// ...and put that hatch pattern to use
const nationalParksStyle = new Style({
  fill: new Fill({
    color: createHatchPattern()
  }),
  stroke: new Stroke({
    color: '#000000',
    width: 1
  })
});
```

- [ ] Assign this new style to the `tanzania_national_parks_2023* GeoJSON layer, in the same way as the previous one. 



::: {.callout-note}
## Checkpoint

Before continuing, make sure that:

- Forest reserve categories have different colours.
- National parks use a hatch pattern.
- The national parks style is assigned to the correct layer.
- The map still loads without JavaScript errors.
:::
